extracted.intended_audience: manufacturers, testing laboratories, industry stakeholders, regulatory counsel, and commenters on DOE water heater rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Supplemental notice of proposed rulemaking (SNOPR) from DOE proposing amended definitions and standards for circulating water heaters, describing test procedure implications, classification decisions, and procedural requirements for public comment and regulatory review. Intended to solicit data/comments and set regulatory requirements for manufacturers and other stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed definition of 'Circulating water heater' (§430.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Circulating water heater means a water heater that does not have an operational scheme in which the burner, heating element, or compressor initiates and/or terminates heating based on sensing flow; has a water temperature sensor located at the inlet or the outlet of the water heater or in a separate storage tank that is the primary means of initiating and terminating heating; and must be used in combination with a recirculating pump to circulate water and either a separate storage tank or water circulation loop in order to achieve the water flow and temperature conditions recommended in the manufacturer's installation and operation instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the exact proposed regulatory text to be added at §430.2; it sets the definitional criteria that determine product classification, testing approach, and applicability of storage-type standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of circulating water heaters as storage-type (no separate product classes)
rubrics_metrics.description: DOE proposes not to establish separate product classes for circulating water heaters; rather, these products would be included in the applicable storage water heater product classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOE's tentative determination is that circulating water heaters' consumer utility and characteristics align with storage-type water heaters; thus the same standards apply and there is no incentive to re-label storage heaters as circulating heaters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appendix E UFHWST test pairing volume requirement (80–120 gallons)
rubrics_metrics.description: DOE's test procedure in appendix E requires that gas-fired circulating water heaters be tested with an UFHWST having a volume between 80 and 120 gallons (see section 4.10 of appendix E).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-classification and effective storage volume matters: when tested with an UFHWST of 80–100 gallons, the effective storage volume corresponds to condensing-level standards; when tested with an UFHWST of 100–120 gallons, the proposed standards correspond to noncondensing efficiencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: thermostatically-activated (circulating) vs flow-activated (instantaneous)
rubrics_metrics.description: Circulating water heaters are defined as being thermostatically activated and not flow-activated. Products with flow-activated control schemes must be tested/certified using maximum GPM; products that are not flow-activated use a first-hour rating (FHR) delivery capacity metric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOE tentatively determined circulating water heaters would not be direct substitutes for instantaneous (flow-activated) water heaters based on these control-scheme differences and associated testing/certification metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certification and testing metric: maximum GPM for flow-activated products
rubrics_metrics.description: Products with flow-activated control schemes must be tested for a maximum gallons per minute ("maximum GPM") delivery capacity and must be certified with such in order to determine a draw pattern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOE notes all currently certified gas-fired instantaneous water heaters demonstrate compliance by certifying a maximum GPM, indicating flow-activation; this metric drives applicable test procedures and draw-pattern selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certification and testing metric: First-Hour Rating (FHR) for non-flow-activated products
rubrics_metrics.description: Products that are not flow-activated use a first-hour rating ("FHR") delivery capacity metric and must be certified with such in order to determine a draw pattern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOE observed currently there are no gas-fired instantaneous water heaters certified to DOE with FHR in certain ranges; the FHR vs max-GPM distinction affects which standards/test methods apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer utility as criterion for product class (continuous supply vs storage utility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Storage and instantaneous water heaters offer distinct utilities: instantaneous water heaters provide a continuous supply of hot water up to the maximum flow rate, while storage water heaters are often better suited to handle large initial demands rather than continuous draws. DOE tentatively determined gas-fired circulating water heaters cannot offer continuous supply utility without flow-activated schemes and reliance on recirculation and stored volume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOE requests comment on whether circulating water heaters provide the same consumer utility as instantaneous heaters; consumer utility is pivotal in classification decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Storage-type input rate limits for consumer vs commercial classification
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining if a circulating water heater is a consumer water heater, storage-type input rate limits apply: 75,000 Btu/h for gas-fired circulating water heaters, 105,000 Btu/h for oil-fired circulating water heaters, 12 kW for electric resistance circulating water heaters, and 24 A at 250 V for heat pump circulating water heaters (see definition for “water heater” at 10 CFR 430.2). Products with higher input rates would be commercial water heaters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These numeric thresholds determine whether a model falls in consumer regulation scope or is instead commercial; DOE cites market examples of higher-input gas models that would be commercial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to certify compliance and follow DOE test procedures (10 CFR part 429)
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacturers of consumer water heaters must certify to DOE that their products comply with any applicable energy conservation standards and must test their products according to the DOE test procedures for consumer water heaters, including any amendments adopted for those test procedures. Certification and recordkeeping requirements are governed by 10 CFR part 429.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certification is a legal obligation; DOE enforces via recordkeeping and may inspect or require supporting test reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA) information-collection and estimated burden
rubrics_metrics.description: The collection-of-information requirement for the certification and recordkeeping is subject to review and approval by OMB under the PRA. This requirement has been approved under OMB control number 1910-1400. Public reporting burden for the certification is estimated to average 35 hours per response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submitters should be aware of PRA constraints and OMB control numbers; no person is required to respond to an information collection without a valid OMB control number displayed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public comment submission procedures via regulations.gov
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments, data, and information may be submitted via www.regulations.gov; the web page requires name and contact information. Contact information will be viewable to DOE staff only; publicly visible fields will be first and last names, organization name (if any), and submitter representative name (if any). If contact info is included in the comment itself or attached documents it will be publicly viewable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you do not want personal contact info public, provide it in a cover letter separate from your comment. Keep tracking numbers and expect processing delays with large volumes; regs.gov cannot accept information claimed as CBI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidential Business Information (CBI) submission protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not submit CBI through www.regulations.gov. Pursuant to 10 CFR 1004.11, submitters believing information is confidential should email two well-marked copies: one marked “confidential” with all information, and one marked “non-confidential” with confidential info deleted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOE will make its own determination about confidentiality and treat the information according to that determination. Submitting through regs.gov waives any CBI claim for that submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic submission technical and format requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments/documents submitted electronically should be provided in PDF (preferred), Microsoft Word or Excel, WordPerfect, or text (ASCII). Documents should be in English, free of defects or viruses, not secured/encrypted, and should avoid special characters. If possible, include an electronic signature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These format expectations reduce processing errors and support posting to the public docket; inclusion of restricted info in attachments makes it publicly viewable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Campaign form letters batching guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Submit campaign form letters by the originating organization in batches of between 50 to 500 form letters per PDF or as one form letter with a list of supporters' names compiled into one or more PDFs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduces comment processing and posting time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postal/hand-delivery submission guidance (CDs and no faxes)
rubrics_metrics.description: If submitting via postal mail or hand delivery/courier, provide all items on a CD if feasible; no telefacsimiles ("faxes") will be accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including electronic copies on CD reduces DOE's need to re-key or scan materials and is recommended where practicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: DOE's solicitation of comments on specific issues
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) DOE requests comment on its tentative determination that gas-fired circulating water heaters do not provide the same consumer utility as gas-fired instantaneous water heaters. (2) DOE requests comment on its proposed amended definition for circulating water heaters, and seeks information on whether it is appropriate to classify these products as storage-type water heaters and what the industry implications might be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOE welcomes data, cost or technical information, alternative proposals, and usage/market evidence relevant to these two focal issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Order 12866 / 13563 / 14094 regulatory-review principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals must be: (1) based on a reasoned determination that benefits justify costs (recognizing some benefits/costs are hard to quantify); (2) tailored to impose the least burden consistent with objectives; (3) select approaches that maximize net benefits (including distributive impacts and equity); (4) specify performance objectives where feasible rather than prescriptive compliance means; and (5) identify and assess alternatives including economic incentives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOE emphasizes using best available techniques to quantify benefits/costs (including changes from technological innovation or behavioral changes) and submitted its assessments to OIRA for review as required for significant regulatory actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: OIRA review requirement for significant regulatory actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 6(a) of E.O. 12866 requires agencies to submit 'significant regulatory actions' to OIRA for review. DOE provided OIRA an assessment including underlying analyses of benefits, costs, and alternatives and explained why the planned regulatory action is preferable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOE's July 2023 NOPR was determined a 'significant regulatory action'; corresponding analyses are summarized in the NOPR and detailed in the technical support document (TSD).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) / IRFA requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The RFA requires preparation of an initial regulatory flexibility analysis (IRFA) for any rule required to be proposed for public comment unless the agency certifies the rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. DOE's proposed definition change does not affect the IRFA presented in the July 2023 NOPR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow E.O. 13272 procedures for considering small-entity impacts and make procedures/policies available (DOE reference provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: NEPA categorical exclusion for energy conservation standards rulemakings (B5.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: DOE anticipates this rulemaking qualifies for categorical exclusion B5.1 because it establishes energy conservation standards for consumer products or industrial equipment, none of the exceptions identified in B5.1(b) apply, no extraordinary circumstances exist, and it meets the requirements for application of the categorical exclusion (see 10 CFR 1021.410).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOE will complete its NEPA review before issuing a final rule; if exceptions or extraordinary circumstances exist, a different NEPA analysis may be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unfunded Mandates Reform Act (UMRA) obligations and $100 million threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: UMRA requires agencies to assess effects of regulatory actions on state/local/tribal governments and the private sector. If a proposed rule may result in expenditures of $100 million or more in any one year (adjusted for inflation), the agency must publish a written statement estimating costs, benefits, and other national effects and consider effective intergovernmental consultation and alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOE notes potential private-sector expenditures (R&D, capital, incremental consumer purchases) could exceed the threshold and that the July 2023 NOPR and TSD address UMRA content requirements and alternatives analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Order 12988 drafting and clarity standards
rubrics_metrics.description: When promulgating rules agencies must: (1) eliminate drafting errors and ambiguity, (2) write regulations to minimize litigation, (3) provide a clear legal standard for affected conduct rather than a general standard, (4) promote simplification and burden reduction, (5) clearly specify preemptive effect and any effect on existing Federal law, (6) specify retroactive effect if any, and (7) adequately define key terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOE states it has completed the required review and determined, to the extent permitted by law, the proposed rule meets the standards of E.O. 12988.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information Quality Bulletin for Peer Review (influential scientific information peer review)
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB's Final Information Quality Bulletin for Peer Review establishes that certain scientific information must be peer reviewed before dissemination, including 'influential scientific information' related to agency regulatory actions. Energy conservation standards rulemaking analyses are considered 'influential scientific information.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOE conducted formal peer reviews of the standards-development process and analyses, prepared a report, and engaged the National Academy of Sciences to review analytical methodologies; DOE is evaluating resulting recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Order 13211 energy effects statement requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: E.O. 13211 requires agencies to prepare and submit to OIRA a Statement of Energy Effects for proposed significant energy actions. A 'significant energy action' is one that is a significant regulatory action and likely to have significant adverse effects on energy supply, distribution, or use, or designated as such by OIRA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOE tentatively concluded this regulatory action is not a 'significant energy action' and therefore did not prepare a Statement of Energy Effects.
